source.title: Humans and language models diverge when predicting repeating text
source.authors: Aditya R. Vaidya; Javier Turek; Alexander G. Huth

record.file_problem: None; full paper text is supplied, with minor PDF extraction artifacts.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures induction-like attention in GPT-2 Small and tests its role in repeated-text prediction by adding attention biases. It does not reproduce the original training-time analysis or use the original small attention-only transformer setup.
record.gate_note: The study directly measures induction-like attention and reports repeated-text prediction results. Its layer-bias intervention also reports effects on those results. The training-loss bump, abrupt formation during training, and broad generality across models are not tested.
record.test_reason: The study finds heads with induction attention ([A][B]…[A]→[B] copying across repeats) in a pre-trained GPT-2 Small fine-tuned to word-level tokens. This is a new model setting for whether induction heads appear (V4). It does not test previous-token composition in attention-only models (V1), training dynamics (V2, V7), data dependence (V5), or few-shot task learning (V3, V6).
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that GPT-2's superhuman recall of repeated text arises from heads (from layer 6 on) that attend across presentation boundaries to copy the next token. A power-law recency bias on these heads makes later-presentation predictions more human-like across held-out stimuli, with a small drop (about 0.03 at layer 6) in first-presentation correlation and increased perplexity on non-repeating text. They note that improvements at every layer suggest other mechanisms, or the inputs to induction heads, may matter.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines a pre-trained GPT-2 Small on repeated natural-text spans, inspects attention patterns, and optimizes additive recency biases. It does not analyze induction-head emergence during training in small attention-only transformers.
record.method_sensitivity: Effects vary by intervention layer: improvements are strongest for layers 4–9, with small improvements at every layer. The reported induction pattern emerges at layer 6 and continues through layer 12.

fits_no_version.finding: A recency-bias intervention optimized at any layer, including layers 1–5 before the induction pattern appears, improved human-model correlation on repeated spans. The authors say induction heads may not be the only memory mechanism for copying repeated text.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Verbatim copying of repeated spans in pretrained LMs may depend on mechanisms beyond induction heads, or on their inputs in earlier layers.

fits_no_version.finding: Disrupting layer-6 attention (which weakened induction patterns downstream) raised perplexity on non-repeating text by more than 40%; edits in the earliest and latest layers raised it about 10%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Layers carrying induction-like attention contribute to general next-word prediction on non-repeating text.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Computational Natural Language Learning (2023)
record.problems: The attention-pattern summary is reported without numerical values in the text. The mechanistic test uses GPT-2 Small and does not test previous-token-head composition or training-time formation. The intervention changes attention broadly rather than selectively ablating induction heads.

untested.parts: Composition with an earlier previous-token head, and small attention-only transformers; no circuit analysis is done.
All parts: no training trajectory, loss bump or timing.
All parts: no measure of how much in-context learning induction heads account for, and no large models.
Other families, sizes, training runs, architectures and modalities; only one GPT-2 Small checkpoint is examined.
All parts: training data and setup are not varied.
All parts: no few-shot task learning.

missing.what: Perplexity cost on unseen non-repeating text by intervened layer: more than 40% at layer 6, about 10% in early and late layers, about 15% at layer 9.

record.verdict_notes: The induction-head evidence is qualitative (attention plots), in a single fine-tuned GPT-2 Small checkpoint. The intervention is a broad additive attention bias, not a targeted ablation of induction heads. The reader's V1 links were wrong: the model is not attention-only and composition is not examined.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test composition with an earlier previous-token head, and GPT-2 Small is not described as an attention-only transformer.
No training-time formation trajectory, training-loss bump, or timing comparison with in-context-learning gains is measured.
The study does not test most in-context learning across large transformers; it studies repeated-span prediction in GPT-2 Small.
No comparison across model families, sizes, training runs, architectures, or modalities.
The study does not vary training data or setup to test induction-head formation or persistence of in-context learning.
Few-shot task learning through other heads or mechanisms is not tested.
The study does not track separate formation sub-steps or overlapping training transitions.

rows.operation_detail: Summarized attention probability mass in induction-like attention patterns by layer.

conditions.value: repeating spans used in the study
averaged over all 12 heads, all tokens, and all stimuli

rows.measure: Attention mass on the token after each past instance of the current token
rows.value: Induction-like attention emerges sharply at layer 6 and is present in each subsequent layer through layer 12.
rows.note: The paper describes the pattern by layer but does not state numeric attention-mass values in the text.
rows.check: Relinked from V1 to V4. GPT-2 Small is not a small attention-only transformer, and previous-token composition is not tested. The row shows heads with induction behaviour in another model family. No numeric attention mass is given in the text (Fig 3b only).

rows.stage_stated: pre-trained and fine-tuned to change tokenization to word-level
rows.operation_detail: Inspected the attention matrix for head 1.
rows.measure: Attention to tokens at the repeated-span offset
rows.value: Strong diagonal attention indicates induction; on the third presentation, the head attends to previous instances 64 and 129 tokens in the past.
rows.note: The paper states that these attended-to positions are the tokens that should be output.
rows.check: Relinked from V1 to V4, for the same reason as R1. Example head with offset-64/129 attention in layer 6.

rows.subject: GPT-2 Small
rows.stage_stated: pre-trained and fine-tuned to change tokenization to word-level
rows.operation_detail: Optimized and added a recency-form attention bias to all heads in layer 6 to match human prediction accuracy.
rows.value: Later-presentation performance moved closer to human values; initial-presentation performance was largely unchanged.
rows.uncertainty: SEM across initializations shown in Figure 4b
rows.note: The intervention was optimized on one stimulus and evaluated on held-out stimuli.
rows.check: Measures human-model prediction similarity after the study's own recency-bias optimization. It is not a rate or mechanism of induction heads. It is the study's method result.

rows.subject: GPT-2 Small
rows.stage_stated: pre-trained and fine-tuned to change tokenization to word-level
rows.operation_detail: Added the optimized recency-form attention bias in layer 6 and measured resulting attention-pattern changes.
rows.value: Layer 6 attention on the current token increased at the expense of all other measured patterns, including induction; the induction pattern was also weaker in following layers.
rows.note: The paper reports weakening, not elimination, of the induction pattern.
rows.check: Measures the induction-pattern change caused by the study's own intervention. It does not bear on whether induction heads form or function as a version states.

rows.subject: GPT-2 Small
rows.stage_stated: pre-trained and fine-tuned to change tokenization to word-level
rows.operation_detail: Repeated the attention-bias optimization independently at each layer.
rows.value: Correlation improved regardless of the optimized layer; effects were strongest for layers 4–9, with small improvements in every layer.
rows.note: The paper says this may indicate induction heads are not the only important memory mechanism, or that similar effects can come from modifying their inputs.
rows.check: Measures human-model correlation change under the study's intervention at each layer. The authors offer two incompatible readings, so it bears on no version directly. Recorded under fits_no_version.

rows.subject: GPT-2
rows.stage_stated: fine-tuned to change tokenization to word-level
rows.operation_detail: Measured perplexity across repeated spans in an additional experiment.

conditions.value: 15 or until input exceeded the 1024-token maximum

rows.value: After a few presentations, perplexity quickly plateaus to near-perfect performance; the model effectively memorizes the span.
rows.uncertainty: Standard deviation increases substantially for smaller spans at higher repetitions; numerical values not stated in text.
rows.note: Aggregate result across the 100 spans; the text does not provide exact plotted values.
rows.check: Measures repeated-span perplexity only and attributes nothing to induction heads. The subject is the same word-level fine-tuned GPT-2 Small, not an unspecified 'GPT-2'.

relationships.condition: Pre-trained GPT-2 Small, fine-tuned to word-level tokenization, on repeated natural-text spans
relationships.reason: Multiple heads in layers 6–12 show induction attention to the token after earlier instances (offsets 64 and 129) (R1–R3).
relationships.display_finding: Multiple heads in layers 6–12 attend to tokens following earlier instances, at offsets 64 and 129.
